message.content:
### Your Rights as a Tenant in Texas (as of 2026) | Area | What You’re Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |------|------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • The landlord may hold a maximum of **one month’s rent** (or two if the lease is for a month‑to‑month tenancy).
• The deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any move‑in inspection report.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions if the landlord withholds part of the deposit. | | **Habitability** | • The landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control).
• Repairs must be made within a reasonable time after you notify the landlord. | • Notify the landlord in writing (email or certified mail) and keep a copy.
• If repairs are not made, you may withhold rent, repair and deduct, or file a complaint with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA). | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable (usually not more than 5% of the rent). | • Pay on time or negotiate a payment plan if you’re having trouble. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • You have the right to live without unreasonable interference from the landlord or other tenants. | • Report any harassment or unlawful entry. | | **Entry by Landlord** | • The landlord must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) before entering, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of all entries. | | **Lease Termination** | • For month‑to‑month leases, either party can terminate with **30 days’ written notice**.
• For fixed‑term leases, the landlord can’t terminate early unless you breach the lease or the landlord has a valid reason (e.g., non‑payment, illegal activity). | • Provide written notice and keep copies. | | **Discrimination** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income (e.g., public assistance). | • File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR) if you suspect discrimination. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a habitability issue, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from your rent, provided you follow the proper procedure. | • Keep receipts and provide the landlord with a written notice of the repair and deduction. | | **Eviction Process** | • The landlord must follow the Texas eviction procedure: serve a **Notice to Pay Rent or Quit** (10 days for non‑payment) or a **Notice to Cure or Quit** (10 days for lease violations).
• If you fail to comply, the landlord can file an eviction lawsuit. | • Respond to notices promptly; consider legal counsel if facing eviction. | | **Legal Assistance** | • You can seek help from local tenant advocacy groups, legal aid organizations, or the Texas Attorney General’s office. | • Many nonprofits offer free or low‑cost legal advice. | | **Reporting Violations** | • File complaints with the TDHCA for habitability issues or with the TCHR for discrimination. | • Provide documentation (photos, receipts, correspondence). | #### Quick Tips 1. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of the lease, move‑in inspection, rent receipts, and any communication with the landlord. 2. **Know the Timeline** – Texas law sets specific notice periods for entry, rent payment, and lease termination. 3. **Use Written Notices** – Even if you talk to the landlord, put important requests in writing and keep a copy. 4. **Seek Legal Counsel Early** – If you’re facing a dispute, early legal advice can prevent escalation. --- **Disclaimer:** This information is general in nature and not legal advice. For specific situations, consult a licensed attorney or a local tenant advocacy organization.
